events.description: 12. ORDER denying without prejudice 1 Motion For Immediate Injunction. On October 15, 2024, after attempting to file for write-in candidacy, Plaintiff filed this action to request "a judge to make the Secretary of State to accept plaintiff's write-in candidacy." (ECF Nos. 1 .) For the reasons set forth in this ruling, the Court denies without prejudice the requests for injunctive relief.As an initial matter, the Court finds that nothing in the docket shows Plaintiff has effected service of the summons and Complaint upon Defendants. Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(l)(1) ("Unless service is waived, proof of service must be made to the court."); Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(k)(1) ("Serving a summons or filing a waiver of service establishes personal jurisdiction over a defendant.") "A court may not grant a final, or even an interlocutory, injunction over a party over whom it does not have personal jurisdiction." In re Rationis Enters., Inc. of Pan., 261 F.3d 264, 270 (2d Cir. 2001). Because Defendants have neither appeared in this action nor been served with process, the Court denies the request for a preliminary injunction under Rule 65(a) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure at ECF No. 1 .The Court also finds that the request for a temporary restraining order must be denied. A court may issue a temporary restraining order without notifying "the adverse party or its attorney only if: (A) specific facts in an affidavit or verified complaint clearly show that immediate and irreparable injury, loss, or damage will result to the movant before the adverse party can be heard in opposition; and (B) the movant's attorney certified in writing any efforts made to give notice and the reasons why is should not be required." Fed. R. Civ. P. 65(b)(1). These requirements are stringent and must be scrupulously honored. Fed. Trade Comm'n v. Grand Teton Pros., LLC, No. 3:19-CV-933 (VAB), 2019 WL 4439501, at *2 (D. Conn. June 18, 2019). Here, Plaintiff has failed to comply with the stringent requirements of Rule 65. Even under a liberal construction of the filings, the Court cannot discern "that immediate and irreparable injury, loss, or damage will result to the movant before the adverse party can be heard in opposition," as required by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65(b)(1)(A). Therefore, the Court cannot grant Plaintiff an ex parte temporary restraining order. Moreover, even if Plaintiff complied with Rule 65, it is unclear how the request satisfies the purpose of "preserv[ing] an existing situation in statu quo until the court has an opportunity to pass upon the merits of the demand for a preliminary injunction." Garcia v. Yonkers School Dist., 561 F.3d 97, 107 (2d Cir. 2009) (internal quotation marks and citations omitted).Accordingly, the Court denies Plaintiff's requests for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction without prejudice. Signed by Judge Vernon D. Oliver on 10/22/2024.(Dao, J) (Entered: 10/22/2024)

events.description: 16. ORDER DISMISSING CASE. In October 2024, after attempting to file for write-in candidacy, Plaintiff filed this action to request "a judge to make the Secretary of State to accept plaintiff's write-in candidacy." (ECF No. 1 .) For the reasons set forth in this ruling, the Court concludes that the Complaint must be DISMISSED WITHOUT PREJUDICE to refiling in state court."[A] court must satisfy itself that it has subject matter jurisdiction and may at any time in the course of litigation consider whether such jurisdiction exists." Mitskovski v. Buffalo & Fort Erie Pub. Bridge Auth., 435 F.3d 127, 133 (2d Cir. 2006). If necessary, where jurisdiction is questionable, a court may examine its subject matter jurisdiction sua sponte. Joseph v. Leavitt, 465 F.3d 87, 89 (2d Cir. 2006). "[T]he plaintiff asserting subject matter jurisdiction has the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that it exists." Luckett v. Bure, 290 F.3d 493, 497 (2d Cir. 2002).Plaintiff does not properly allege this Court's subject matter jurisdiction. First, as to federal question jurisdiction, "[f]ederal district courts have subject-matter jurisdiction over 'all civil actions arising under the Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States.' " Gallego v. Northland Grp. Inc., 814 F.3d 123, 126 (2d Cir. 2016) (quoting 28 U.S.C. § 1331). Even under a liberal construction of the Complaint, the Court cannot discern that this action arises under federal law. Instead, Plaintiff appears to bring this action under a state statute governing the registration of write-in candidates, Conn. Gen. Stat. § 9-373a.Second, as to diversity jurisdiction, federal district courts have diversity jurisdiction over actions where there is complete diversity among parties and an amount in controversy in excess of $75,000. 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a). Neither requirement is plausibly alleged in the Complaint. Because the parties appear to be residents of Connecticut, that precludes a finding of complete diversity that would establish diversity jurisdiction. And the Complaint fails to demonstrate a reasonable probability that the amount in controversy requirement is satisfied.It is axiomatic that federal courts have limited jurisdiction and must dismiss actions where subject matter jurisdiction is absent. See Nike, Inc. v. Already, LLC, 663 F.3d 89, 94 (2d. Cir. 2011). Accordingly, the case is DISMISSED WITHOUT PREJUDICE for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(h)(3). Because this action was filed in federal court, as opposed to removed from state court, the Court cannot remand the case. Plaintiff may file another action in state court. The Clerk is respectfully directed to close the case. All pending motions are denied as moot.Signed by Judge Vernon D. Oliver on 10/25/2024. (Dao, J) (Entered: 10/25/2024)
